item.title: Algeria
item.description:
About

Algeria features a diverse landscape that includes mountain ranges, vast deserts, and karstic plateaus, making it highly relevant from a speleological and geological perspective.

🪨 Limestone Karst in Algeria

Yes, Algeria has significant limestone karst formations, especially in the northern and northeastern regions of the country. These include:

  • Djurdjura Mountains (part of the Tell Atlas): This region has well-developed karst plateaus with numerous caves and sinkholes, formed in Jurassic and Cretaceous limestones.
  • **Constantine and Setif regions**: Known for complex karst systems and underground hydrology.
  • Tassili n’Ajjer (southeastern Algeria - DO NOT TRAVEL): While primarily known for its sandstone formations and prehistoric rock art, some karst-like erosion features occur in isolated carbonate outcrops.

🕳️ Caves in Algeria

Algeria has extensive cave systems, many of which are of speleological, ecological, or archaeological interest. Notable caves include:

item.title: Allendale - 5L11
item.description:
From CaveDB

Known as the ‘hole in the middle of the road’, Allendale is one the of the first CDAA Cave Rated sites that divers have access in the earlier steps of their cave training. The cave consists of a main straight tunnel on a 45 degrees slope reaching 26m depth at the bottom and a total 60m length (from surface to deepest part). A small surface lake can host divers comfortably with water level usually at below waist level. The Northwest corner of the lake will grant access to the cave’s main tunnel which is reasonably large until you reach 12m depth after a 25m swim. Attentive divers will notice on their right hand side that some sort of collapse happened there. The main tunnel branches East at the 12 m restriction, and one can navigate through a narrow passage until hitting a full stop after a roughly 15 metres swim. Back to the main tunnel and once cleared the 12m depth mark, divers will face a large room spanning 30m in length (to the deepest part of the cave) and 20m in width. Behind the black silt pile on the Northwest corner a fissure on the rock has been object of many divers work. She doesn’t go, yet…

item.title: Allendale East Cave – Soggy Wombats
item.description:
Allendale East Cave

Introduction

Known as the hole in the middle of the road or just ‘the Dale’, Allendale East Cave is a very popular site among the CDAA Cave rated divers in the Mount Gambier region. As it presents itself as a non-complex cave to dive in, the Soggy Wombats Team has been training, developing skills and accumulating experience in this cave since 2019. Although geographically far from the most developed cave systems in the region, ‘the Dale’ has a small ‘tunnel’ at it’s deepest end that has been in most of Australian’s Cave Divers dreams to break into something big. There hasn’t been any breakthrough in this cave in the last 20 years or so, but with the advances in exploration techniques, we might be surprised with what the future will tell us.

item.title: Article - Corra-Lynn
item.description: When I tell people I’ve just met that I’m a cave diver with claustrophobia, I always get a few confused looks followed by an inevitable round of questions along the lines of “Oh, so how do you stop the panic then?”. But when I mention my claustrophobia to people who know me and the kind of cave diving I do, the reaction is generally more like “You are very clearly broken, Josh - what is wrong with your brain?”.

item.title: Article - Iddlebiddy Cave - Soggy Wombats - DRAFT
item.description:
Introduction

First discovered sometime in the early 1980’s by an enthusiastic band of unqualified local divers, Iddlebiddy Cave was named as a tongue-in-cheek nod to far larger Cocklebiddy Cave on the Nullarbor Plains which is resembles in structure if not in size. The location of Iddlebiddy Cave remained a closely guarded secret for several years, until it was first formally surveyed on 26 November 1988 by Tony Hambling, Frank Homewood and John McCormick on behalf of the Cave Divers Association of Australia.

The site features a vertical solution tube approximately 1 meter in diameter, descending around 16 meters to reach the water. Divers can swim to a clean rock in waist-deep water, which serves as a stable platform for donning or doffing dive gear.

The dive itself includes a spacious underwater main chamber that connects to a tunnel reaching a maximum depth of 33 meters.

item.title: Cocklebiddy Cave - 6N48
item.description:
From ASF

About

Cocklebiddy Cave is over 6.5km long and is the longest single underwater passage in Australia. The entrance is in a degraded doline 120m long and a steep talus slope beneath overhang at the North end leads to large chamber 360 x 45 x 30m high with 180m long lake. The lake contains “mud islands”.

It is possible to snorkel the lake to look down at the first sump, the water can be muddy after rain.

item.title: Fossil Cave - 5L81
item.description:
From CaveDB

Fossil cave is named for the fossils found there so care must be taken not to disturb these. It is a doline collapse that has east and west dives. The west side is a shortish cave level dive that has many nooks and cranies to explore. The west is bigger and rated cave for the most part but there is a restriction at 13m that you must be cave rated to pass and enters the tank cave system.

item.title: Goa Lalauwi
item.description:
Other Descriptions

About

From Anita: - This is a cave that deserves a special mention. A 600m submerged tunnel leads into the heart of the cave. So far around 3km of tunnels have been explored, yet the cave keeps on going. Goa Lalauwi keeps a few secrets up its sleeve as it wants you to come back for more. On my first dive we swam through big tunnels with white limestone, sections of fractured rock and large areas of stalagmites in crystal clear blue water. To get to the water you walk over 100 steps down a dry chamber which means the cave it self is never exposed to any sunlight. It’s pitch black. This means you are reliant on your torch as soon as you step into the cave. It is quite slippery at the entrance lake and you need to take care not to slip and fall. Then you kit up inside the lake aided by your torch light before the descent towards the first tunnel. The second dive in this beauty was far more complex from a navigational perspective with lots of directional decisions and several jumps that lead to a section with little white humps in the form of witches’ hats. According to our guide, these formations are considered quite rare and, unlike the other speleothems in the caves, form under water. While I have spent several hours in this cave, I will be back for more.

item.title: Gua La Pahia
item.description:
Other Descriptions

To Do

Diving Dry Photogrammetry

About

“The House Cave” for Kadena Glamping Muna

  • From Anita:
    • “In the backyard of where we stayed lies Goa La Pahia, the hidden cave, with an unassuming small rock entrance surrounded by vegetation. As you descend, it slowly unveils its secrets. Calcite crystal formations decorate the ceiling. which tum into whole sections covered in crystal straws. As you swim further along the cave it reveals more and more of its unique formations. Small but impressive, it has a special place in my heart. The first underwater crystal cave that I have ever seen was a dream come true. The sheer beauty, uniqueness and the masses of speleothems took a while to sink in. I was on such a high, but at the same time I was so calm and close to a meditative state as I took in the surroundings with awe and wonder. This was my introduction to cave diving in Muna Island. What a phenomenal start that made me curious for what lay in store for the coming days.”

item.title: Iddlebiddy Cave - 5L250
item.description:
From CaveDB

Iddlebiddy Cave is a 250m single passage-way, which runs from the entrance chamber and ends in a small, silty room containing an array of largely-formed clay deposits.

Divers must take care when venturing into this cave, as the soft walls and delicate features located in the long passage make the water susceptible to clouding. Divers are encouraged to take their time passing through the passage, to enjoy the many cave features and avoid causing finning or physical damage.

item.title: Kilbsy's Sinkhole - 5L46
item.description:
From CaveDB

Kilsby Sinkhole is a naturally occurring karst sinkhole located on private property 10 kilometres south-west of Mount Gambier in South Australia. The sinkhole is renowned worldwide for its crystal clear water and extensive open caverns, making it a popular destination for recreational diving. The site is accessible only via prior bookings, which can be made online or by phone.

Kilsby Sinkhole is the only site of its kind in Australia that welcomes snorkellers and Open Water certified divers, through to those with Cave or Technical dive training. Snorkellers, Freedivers and Open Water divers must be guided by an approved Dive Instructor. With a depth of almost 30 metres directly from the pontoon, the site is a perfect location for freediving and training camps are regularly held onsite.

item.title: Little Blue Lake - 5L9
item.description:
From CaveDB

Little Blue is a commonly used as a local swimming hole as well as being a popular basic cave diving site. It is relatively easy to access from the road and has a decent equipment assembly table and stairs running straight down to the water. The clarity can be quite poor and it is relatively deep getting down to nearly 40m. You should take care on your air consumption and non deco time as you will run into deco quite quickly. Visibility can be quite poor especially in the top 20m and there is little to see beyond random junk that has been thrown into it over the years. The rubbish include barbed wire and other random items so take care around the bottom not to get snagged. During summer months it can be full of locals swimming and dive bombing from the top so be careful not to get landed on.

item.title: Moko Morete
item.description:
From CaveDB

Moko Morete opens in a vast blue hole. An underwater passage to the west can be followed 10 to 15 m, but then it becomes too narrow. It may lead to Gua Moko. The main passage begins to the east. With 403 m, it is one of the longest sumps explored on Muna so far. The maximum depth is 21 m. The inner part is huge, ending in a collapse due to the very soft nature of the limestone. The cave still needs to be thoroughly explored. Only the few first meters are exposed to daylight.

item.description:
Other Descriptions

About

Also known as Cocklebiddy 3 Mile Cave, the entrance is a small overhanging doline 20m in diameter. A 20m pitch leads to a loose talus and silt slope which becomes a boulder floored passage after the doline. The passage continues to a small lake at 89m. There are wetas near the entrance of the cave. There was a thylacine carcase found on early trips to the cave.

item.title: Nettlebed - 5L290
item.description:
From CaveDB

Nettlebed Cave is home to a range of interesting features for cave divers to explore. The wall-scratchings which can seen once inside “The Gallery” are probable evidence of megafauna, while entrenched seashells provide insight into the cave’s Ice Age inhabitants.

Beyond The Gallery, the cave drops deeper and breaks into additional rooms containing many large, dark silt-covered boulders, black walls and white-clay floored passages.

The cave finishes in a chamber at 28m, but with an actual penetration distance from the surface of 80m.

item.title: Nurina Cave
item.description:
From CaveDB

Situated to the east of Madura Pass, approximately 1400km from Perth, you’ll find a fascinating cave on the Roe Plain. Here, the limestone surface is in close proximity to the water table. This underwater cave is a complex network of intersecting fissures, with a generally small breakdown passage. It features distinct bedding planes at depths of 3, 5, and 7 meters, which house stunning horizontal elliptical phreatic passages as well as low flat passages, all interconnected. The deepest point is a 7m bedding plane, and so far, 410m of underwater passage has been explored (as of February 2004).

item.description:
From CaveDB

Overview

Located in the vast expanse of the Nullarbor desert, over 2500 km from Melbourne, Australia, lies a hidden gem known as the Olwolgin Cave. This underwater cave system, named after a nearby bluff on the Roe Plain escarpment, is a fascinating destination for adventurous divers and explorers.

Getting there

The journey to Olwolgin Cave is an adventure in itself. It begins with meticulous packing for a road trip to the middle of nowhere. The route takes you through major multilane highways, rolling hills, and farmed greenery, before the landscape gives way to the single-lane highway snaking along the southern coastline of the continent.

item.title: Tank Cave - 5L230
item.description:
From CaveDB

Tank cave in Mount Gambia, South Australia is one of Australia’s most popular and largest mapped submerged cave. It has over 7km of passage of which most contain fixed lines. It is located in farmland about 20km outside Mount Gambia and its entrance is on land owned by the Cave Divers Association of Australia. The cave is a complex system of interconnected tunnels that requires complex navigation and even after gaining the needed advance cave standard you need to follow a strict familiarization schedule consisting of 18 dives that progressively expand your experience of the system. Care must be taken with planning and cookie discipline due the complexity of dives and particular care taken not to cut corners and potentially miss an obscured branch of line. A large amount of the cave are accessible to back-mount divers but many sections required side-mount configuration to penetrate. Water temperature is relatively constant 14 Celsius year round and a dry suit with suitable thermal protected is needed. Much of the cave is quite shallow around 10-12 metres with deeper sections as you get to the Fossil Cave side getting to 20+ metres.

item.title: The Shaft - 5L158
item.description:
From CaveDB

The Shaft is a sinkhole located near Mount Gambier in South Australia. It is a popular destination for cave divers, known for its clear water and interesting internal structure.

The Shaft is the site of a tragic scuba diving incident that occurred on May 28, 1973, which claimed the lives of four recreational scuba divers. The incident led to the formation of the Cave Divers Association of Australia and the development of the South Australian Police Underwater Recovery Squad .

item.description:
Other Descriptions

About

The entrance to the cave is a large doline 50m in diameter. The obvious route into the doline leads to short cave below the Northwest cliff line.

The main cave has been described as a “wombat- sized hole” which is found in the Southeast end of the doline, about 3m down from the level of the plain. There is a visitor book on a rock shelf in the entrance. The way on is not obvious and goes through a rock squeeze at the end of the low entrance chamber.
